results.reason: Issue 3 contrasts MSA §1.3 (delivery at Rochester) with Schedule §1.1 (shipment from Supplier's plant, bill of lading). It explains that on-time performance, late-delivery and cover remedies, risk of loss, cargo insurance and invoicing all key off the shipment date, so transit delays fall on Harlow.
The fix conforms Schedule §1.1 to the MSA definition (delivery at Harlow's Rochester facility) and adds an order-of-precedence clause making the MSA prevail over the Schedule.

Issue 2 identifies MSA §4.3 as covering all housings and similar components worldwide, against the Term Sheet's Series 7, U.S.-only bargain. It explains the worldwide lock-in and the bar on other sourcing, and recommends narrowing to Series 7 Housings purchased in the United States.

Issue 6 notes §15.2 lets Supplier assign freely, including to a competitor or a thinly capitalized entity, while Customer needs consent. It flags the supply continuity and confidential-specification risks, and recommends requiring Harlow's consent or, at minimum, a termination right and exclusivity release on assignment or change of control.

Issue 1 explains that Amendment §2.1 and §2.2 restate §11.2 to cover willful misconduct only and subject gross negligence and the IP indemnity to the cap. It recommends restoring the original §11.2 carve-outs.
The memo states the cap is the prior 12 months' fees and lists the original §11.2 exclusions as gross negligence, willful misconduct and the IP indemnity (§10.1).
The memo cites Term Sheet §§3.1–3.3 (Series 7 Housings only, within the United States) as the baseline for comparing MSA §4.3.

New York governing law appears in the header and in the governing-law discussion (§16). The memo includes an assumptions section and flags that the legal principles need verification. Its only statute reference, UCC §2-305, is real and falls within that flag; no fabricated cases.

The memo is addressed to the partner and organized issue by issue, each with Where / Why it matters / Fix headings. Issues are ordered by importance, and there is a dedicated assumptions and facts-needed section.

The Term Sheet is used only as the baseline for the agreed deal and is never proposed for correction. The 3-year term and 45-day payment terms are not treated as defects; the memo only advises calendaring the dispute deadlines.

Exclusivity is correctly attributed to MSA §4.3 and assignment to §15.2, with the correct party benefiting. Legal principles are flagged for verification. Minor slips (e.g., calling the IP indemnity 'cap-exempt' in the insurance point) do not misattribute the core problems.
